## Key ATCR Metrics and Definitions
### Flight Cancellation Rate
**Definition:** The percentage of scheduled flights that were cancelled, not including diverts (flights that landed at an airport other than their scheduled destination due to weather/emergency).
**2024 Performance:** Full-year 2024 cancellation rate was 1.4%, up from 1.3% in 2023. For December 2024, the cancellation rate was 0.7%, compared with 0.5% in November 2024 and 0.4% in December 2023 (BTS ATCR full-year 2024).
**Trend Interpretation:** Full-year 2024 cancellations of 1.4% sit above the 2023 rate of 1.3% but below the 2019 rate of 1.9%, reflecting ongoing variability across the post-pandemic period. Cancellation rates vary year to year; attributing specific causes (weather, National Airspace System constraints, carrier operational events) requires DOT/FAA delay-cause and local operations data beyond the headline ATCR cancellation figure (BTS ATCR, 2019–2024).
Post-2022, cancellation rates improved from 2.71% in 2022 to 1.3% in 2023, before edging up to 1.4% in 2024; isolating the drivers of year-to-year changes requires DOT/FAA delay-cause data beyond the headline cancellation figure.

## Key ATCR Metrics and Definitions
### Mishandled Baggage Rate
**Definition:** Since January 2019, the mishandled baggage rate has used checked bags handled as its denominator (not passengers enplaned, as was used prior to 2019). DOT has displayed the rate as a percentage of bags enplaned since January 2022; for the 2019–2021 reports it was published per 1,000 checked bags. This guide expresses the rate per 1,000 checked bags for readability (0.55% equals 5.5 per 1,000). A "mishandled" report includes lost, damaged, or delayed luggage. The denominator change means post-2019 figures are not directly comparable to pre-2019 data.
**2024 Performance:** December 2024 mishandled baggage rate was 6.0 per 1,000 checked bags handled, up from 3.9 in November 2024 and 5.0 in December 2023. Full-year 2024 average was approximately 5.5 per 1,000 checked bags handled (0.55%) per BTS ATCR full-year 2024.
**Seasonal Pattern:** Peak months (Jun–Dec) average higher rates due to volume surges and handling complexity; December 2024 reached 6.0 per 1,000 checked bags (0.60%). Shoulder months show lower rates (3–4 per 1,000 range) (BTS ATCR, 2024).
**Observed Range:** Based on 2024 ATCR monthly data, rates ranged from approximately 3 per 1,000 checked bags in shoulder months to a summer peak of about 7.5 per 1,000 in July (0.75%), with December at 6.0 per 1,000. Carriers and months with rates above the 5.5 full-year average warrant closer review; rates well below the annual average indicate above-average handling performance for that period. For carrier-level baggage data, consult the BTS ATCR carrier tables in the applicable monthly or annual report.

## Key ATCR Metrics and Definitions
### Involuntary Denied Boarding Rate
**Definition:** Involuntary denied boardings (IDB) per 10,000 passengers (boardings), reported quarterly under 14 CFR Part 250. This is distinct from voluntary denied boarding, where the airline offers compensation and passengers voluntarily give up their seats.
**2024 Performance:** Involuntary denied boarding rate in 2024 was 0.28 per 10,000 passengers (BTS ATCR full-year 2024). That is modestly above the 0.24 per 10,000 recorded for full-year 2019 (BTS ATCR full-year 2019), but both rates remain very low by historical standards, reflecting carriers' more conservative overbooking practices since 2019.
**Regulatory Context:** Airlines are required to disclose involuntary denial rates publicly and to compensate denied passengers under DOT regulations. Effective January 22, 2025, IDB compensation caps are 200% of the one-way fare (maximum $1,075) for shorter qualifying delay windows, and 400% (maximum $2,150) for longer qualifying delay windows. For domestic air transportation the long-delay threshold is two hours; for covered foreign air transportation the threshold is four hours (14 CFR §250.5). Involuntary denied boardings fell at several carriers in 2025: per 10,000 passengers, Southwest went from 0.08 in 2024 to 0.01 and Spirit from 0.47 to 0.20 (ATCR, February 2026).

## Key ATCR Metrics and Definitions
### Consumer Complaints
**Definition:** For 2024 annual data, DOT's OACP reported consumer submissions — complaints, inquiries, and opinions — as raw counts by carrier and industry group, not as a passenger-normalized complaint rate. Prior to June 2023, the ATCR reported complaints as a rate per 100,000 passengers enplaned. The two series are not directly comparable. Categories include flight problems, reservations, ticketing, refunds, baggage, disabilities, customer service, and other. _Note: In August 2025, DOT launched the Aviation Complaint, Enforcement, and Reporting System (ACERS) (USDOT, Aug. 13, 2025), which updated the taxonomy to complaints, compliments, and comments; the 2024 annual data referenced in this article reflects the pre-ACERS submissions framework._
**2024 Performance:** Full-year 2024 consumer submissions to DOT (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) totaled 97,906, slightly above the 96,853 submissions reported for 2023 (DOT OACP, 2024 Annual Consumer Submissions Data); DOT revised its ATCR reporting to "consumer submissions" terminology as of June 2023. Complaint volumes under the prior complaint-only series peaked in 2020 (102,560 complaints) before declining; the post-June 2023 consumer-submissions series (which includes inquiries and opinions) is broader and not directly comparable to pre-2023 complaint counts (DOT OACP).
**Complaint Category Breakdown:** DOT OACP categorizes consumer submissions into categories including flight problems (delays, cancellations, diversions), refunds, customer service, baggage, reservations/ticketing, and other. For current category-level data, consult the DOT OACP Annual Consumer Submissions Data report directly, as category distributions vary year to year. Post-COVID, refund complaints increased due to confusion about refund policies and implementation delays; flight problem complaints have remained a leading category.

## Data Sources and Reporting Requirements (14 CFR Part 234)
ATCR data comes from multiple regulatory filing streams. The primary sources by metric are:
*   **On-time performance, cancellations, diversions, and baggage handling:** Carrier filings under 14 CFR Part 234 (BTS) — applicable to certificated carriers accounting for ≥0.5% of domestic scheduled passenger revenues.  
*   **Oversales / involuntary denied boarding:** Carrier filings under 14 CFR Part 250, submitted to DOT/BTS under applicable BTS reporting directives — reported quarterly; OACP uses the data in ATCR consumer-protection reporting.  
*   **Tarmac delays:** Consumer-protection requirements and contingency-plan rules under 14 CFR Part 259 (OACP); tarmac delay incident data reported to BTS/OAI under 14 CFR Part 234 for reporting carriers' scheduled domestic flights and 14 CFR Part 244 (Reporting Tarmac Delay Data) for other covered operations — Part 244 §244.2(b)(2) excludes Part 234-reported domestic flights — covering flights held on tarmac beyond applicable thresholds.  
*   **Consumer complaints:** Submitted directly to OACP by passengers and compiled monthly by DOT’s Office of Aviation Consumer Protection.
Carriers file data to the BTS via automated submission, and BTS publishes aggregate reports monthly. The reporting requirement has been in place since 1987 (nine years after the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978), making it one of the most consistent government data sources.
**Reporting Carriers:** Not all airlines are required to file under Part 234. The Part 234 reporting universe consists of certificated carriers accounting for ≥0.5% of domestic scheduled passenger revenues — Southwest and other low-cost carriers, ultra-low-cost carriers such as Frontier and Allegiant, and major network carriers. Foreign carriers are not Part 234 reporting carriers for domestic on-time and baggage data; they appear in ATCR consumer-protection contexts (tarmac delays, complaints) under separate regulatory frameworks. Charter-only operators are not covered.

## Historical Trends: 2019 vs. 2023 vs. 2024
Long-term trends in ATCR metrics reveal industry evolution and operational challenges. All specific percentages and counts in this guide use full-year 2024 as the most recent complete year for worked comparison; DOT has since published full-year 2025 data, which may show different levels and patterns, so practitioners should pull the latest year when benchmarking (DOT OACP; BTS).

## Historical Trends: 2019 vs. 2023 vs. 2024
### On-Time Performance Trends
| **Year** | **On-Time Rate** | **Cancellation Rate** | **Notes** |  
| --- | --- | --- | --- |  
| **2019 (Pre-Pandemic)** | 79.0% | 1.9% | Baseline for normal operations |  
| **2023** | 78.34% | 1.3% | Post-pandemic; recovery ongoing |  
| **2024** | 78.10% | 1.4% | ~1 percentage point below 2019 levels (BTS ATCR) |
**Interpretation:** On-time performance in 2024 is below 2019 baselines and has not improved despite four years of post-pandemic recovery. The industry remains approximately 1 percentage point below 2019 levels (BTS ATCR). Cancellation rates increased 0.1 percentage point year-over-year. Contributing factors may include labor staffing, weather volatility, and fleet age, though the headline ATCR figures alone do not isolate these drivers.

## Historical Trends: 2019 vs. 2023 vs. 2024
### Baggage Handling Trends
BTS changed the mishandled baggage denominator in January 2019 from revenue passengers enplaned to checked bags handled. Under the current (post-2019) methodology, full-year 2024 was approximately 5.5 per 1,000 checked bags (0.55%), with rates ranging from about 3 to 7.5 across months (BTS ATCR, 2024). Pre-2019 figures using the passenger denominator are not directly comparable to post-January-2019 checked-bag-denominator rates. The methodology change reflects the more operationally relevant denominator: baggage handling performance is driven by the number of bags processed, not the number of passengers.

## Historical Trends: 2019 vs. 2023 vs. 2024
### Complaint Trends
Consumer complaints spiked during 2020–2021 due to pandemic-era refund disputes, flight cancellations, and reduced service levels. As of June 2023, DOT revised its ATCR reporting to a "consumer submissions" framework encompassing complaints, inquiries, and opinions — meaning the post-2023 consumer-submissions series is not directly comparable to the pre-2023 complaint-only series. DOT reported 97,906 total consumer submissions in 2024 under this broader reporting scope (DOT OACP, 2024 Annual Consumer Submissions Data).

## Carrier Rankings and Performance Variation
While the ATCR publishes aggregate industry data, it also ranks individual carriers on key metrics. In 2024, carrier rankings showed meaningful variation across carriers (BTS ATCR carrier rankings, 2024):
**On-Time Performance Leaders (2024):** In 2024, carriers varied substantially in on-time performance, with the strongest carriers above the 78.1% industry average and weaker performers below it; the per-carrier figures are in the BTS ATCR carrier rankings, 2024.
**Baggage Handling Leaders:** ATCR baggage metrics describe airline operational performance (handling systems, transfer complexity, staffing), not airport financial or cost-center methodology. Carriers with lower connection complexity (for example, point-to-point operators) typically operate fewer baggage transfers per passenger and tend to post lower mishandled-baggage rates than hub-and-spoke network carriers; carrier-level figures are published in the BTS ATCR carrier tables. Differences across carriers reflect airline operational differences rather than airport ratemaking choices (which govern how airport costs are allocated to airlines, not how airlines handle bags).
**Complaint Rate Leaders:** Analysts sometimes compare these metrics across carriers, but the ATCR itself does not establish a relationship between on-time/baggage performance and complaint rates — any directional pattern is observational and is not quantified in the report's tables. Complaint rates may also reflect factors such as stricter baggage policies and ancillary-fee structures rather than operational quality alone, illustrating that complaint behavior has multiple drivers beyond the two operational metrics.
Airport operators may review carrier rankings in the ATCR to understand which partners are delivering high service quality. Carriers disclose fleet age, staffing, and other operational factors in Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) 10-K filings (e.g., 2024 filings), which can help airports interpret declining ATCR metrics at a given hub.

## Airport Planning and Terminal Design Implications
ATCR data can inform airport facility planning and operations when combined with traffic, financial, and capital-program analysis:

## Airport Planning and Terminal Design Implications
### Gate and Seating Allocation
ATCR system-level trends and BTS T-100 traffic/segment data can be reviewed together to assess whether operational performance changes coincide with capacity or network adjustments — though ATCR reports carrier-system performance, not route-level data, and establishing local causality requires additional analysis. FAA Aviation System Performance Metrics (ASPM) can help airports compare delay, taxi-time, arrival and departure rates, and cancellation patterns when evaluating whether local capacity constraints warrant further study. Carrier-system ATCR trends are at most a screening signal here — they cannot by themselves identify a local gate constraint. Diagnosing one requires airport-specific operational evidence (gate utilization, turn times, ASPM/local delay data, station-level airline data) before a possible gate renovation or expansion is even considered for the capital program. ATCR data is one input among many: capital decisions must also balance financial position, capital needs, and competitive airline rates — gate expansion raises the revenue requirement (debt service, depreciation, O&M) for the affected cost centers, which flows through the rate formula and ultimately into airline payments measured as cost per enplaned passenger (CPE), and the case for any specific project depends on traffic forecasts, bond covenants, airline-use-agreement (AUA) terms, and majority-in-interest (MII) consultation alongside the operational signal.

## Airport Planning and Terminal Design Implications
### Baggage System Capacity
Mishandled baggage rates tend to rise during peak-volume periods, an observational pattern visible in BTS ATCR seasonal data. Confounders include airline staffing levels, fleet age, baggage-system technology vintage, and weather concentration. In 2024 and other recent years, peak-season surges (summer, December holidays) have coincided with elevated cancellation and baggage rates relative to annual averages, though the magnitude varies significantly by month — July 2024 cancellations reached 2.9% (vs. the 1.4% annual average) while December 2024 baggage was 6.0 per 1,000 (vs. 5.5 annual average) (BTS ATCR, 2024). These patterns reflect a combination of uncontrollable (weather, volume) and controllable (airline staffing, scheduling) factors. ATCR baggage data is reported at the carrier level, not by airport. Baggage-system planning should therefore pair it with local baggage-system throughput logs, airline station data, and connection-bank analysis; any capacity upgrade should also be evaluated against capital-program affordability and airline-rate impact per the balance-triangle framework.

## Airport Planning and Terminal Design Implications
### Staffing and Concession Planning
Peak travel seasons (summer, December holidays) coincide with periods of operational strain — cancellation and baggage rates tend to run above annual averages, though the magnitude varies by month and year (BTS ATCR, 2024). Ahead of these periods, airports plan the functions they directly control and coordinate with the parties that control the rest: airport-controlled staffing (custodial, airport operations, parking, and curbside management), airline- or contractor-controlled gate and baggage staffing, and TSA-controlled passenger screening. The airport does not staff airline gate operations or the federal screening checkpoints.

## Airport Planning and Terminal Design Implications
### Passenger Experience Monitoring
DOT complaint data is compiled at the carrier level by OACP, not at the airport level. Airport-level consumer satisfaction analysis typically draws on Transportation Security Administration (TSA) wait-time data, airport satisfaction surveys such as J.D. Power and Airports Council International's (ACI) Airport Service Quality (ASQ) program, and carrier-specific complaint tracking — not the ATCR directly. Because OACP/ATCR complaints are compiled at the carrier-system level, they cannot show that complaints "concentrate at a hub" in the first place. Any hub-specific diagnosis must come from local sources — airport satisfaction surveys, station-level complaint logs, local baggage/operations data, TSA wait-time data, and direct airport observation — which can then point to local factors such as gate crowding, baggage-system delays, or concession capacity.

## Connection: Operational Quality, Customer Loyalty, and Revenue Premium
The ATCR is not a loyalty or revenue dataset — it does not measure customer retention, load factor, or revenue. Analysts sometimes treat operational quality and customer-loyalty indicators as moving together across carriers (drawing on airline investor presentations and academic studies), but any such relationship comes from sources beyond the ATCR and is not a causal finding; airline profitability in particular has multiple drivers — cost per available seat mile (CASM), fuel hedging, labor contracts, network design, loyalty-program structure, and ancillary-revenue mix. ATCR metrics are one signal among several:
*   **On-time performance** is an input airlines often track alongside load factors and total revenue per available seat mile (TRASM), though ATCR does not measure these revenue metrics directly; T-100, the DOT origin-and-destination fare survey (DB1B), and airline SEC filings are required for that analysis.  
*   **Baggage mishandling** is tracked by airlines in customer satisfaction reporting (e.g., J.D. Power, ACI surveys) alongside frequent-flyer program data — but these relationships are not directly derivable from ATCR alone.  
*   **Complaint rates** can be compared with brand and loyalty indicators drawn from other datasets, but the ATCR does not establish that relationship; quantifying any linkage requires airline investor disclosures and market research beyond the ATCR.
ATCR deterioration can be a qualitative signal; revenue and competitive implications require separate review of T-100 load factors, DB1B fare data, and airline SEC filings.
For airport finance professionals, this relationship matters as an early-warning signal rather than a predictor: ATCR metrics offer one observational signal of operational stability that airports may track alongside traffic and financial indicators — in some cases, carriers with improving metrics may be strengthening their competitive position, while those with sustained declines may warrant deeper review of SEC filings (10-K disclosures, route filings, fleet announcements). Airline capacity decisions depend on broader strategic factors (hub economics, fleet plans, network restructuring, code-share dynamics, fuel/labor outlook) that can override the operational signal; ATCR data alone is not a standalone forecast of route or capacity cuts at a specific airport.

## How to Access and Download ATCR Data
ATCR reports are free and available from two primary sources:

## How to Access and Download ATCR Data
### Option 1: BTS Newsroom
Navigate to the BTS ATCR newsroom releases. The December 2024 / full-year 2024 release contains links to the full report PDF and carrier-level tables. For older releases, search bts.gov/statistical-releases. Reports are available in PDF format.

## How to Access and Download ATCR Data
### Option 2: DOT Consumer Portal
Navigate to transportation.gov/airconsumer. This portal provides current reports, archive, and additional consumer tools (flight rights information, complaint filing). This is the more consumer-friendly interface.

## How to Access and Download ATCR Data
### Downloading Data for Analysis
ATCR reports are usually published as PDF or HTML. For bulk analysis (e.g., extracting on-time rates for all carriers over 24 months), you can:
*   **Download monthly PDFs manually:** Labor-intensive but direct  
*   **Request data from BTS directly:** Contact BTS at https://www.bts.gov/about-bts/contact-us for bulk historical data exports  
*   **Use BTS data APIs:** BTS provides some data via API; consult documentation for aviation-specific endpoints  
*   **Consult the DOT ATCR archive and BTS:** the DOT OACP report archive and BTS TranStats provide historical ATCR releases and the underlying operational data for research (note that MIT's Airline Data Project covers Form 41 financial data, not ATCR operational metrics)

## Interpreting Seasonal Variation and Controllable vs. Uncontrollable Factors
ATCR metrics vary significantly by season — in 2024, monthly on-time arrival ranged about 17.6 percentage points peak-to-trough (68.4% in July to 86.0% in October) (BTS ATCR, 2024). Distinguish seasonal variation (weather, volume) from controllable factors using BTS seasonal data:

## Interpreting Seasonal Variation and Controllable vs. Uncontrollable Factors
### Uncontrollable Factors
*   **Weather:** Summer thunderstorms in the Southeast, winter snow in the Northeast, and spring/fall severe weather cause delays and cancellations. These are outside airline control.  
*   **Air traffic congestion:** Major hub airports (ATL, DFW, ORD, LAX) can experience congestion-related delays during peak hours; airports can use FAA Aviation System Performance Metrics (ASPM) data to examine local congestion patterns. Airports control physical infrastructure and common-use gate policy; airlines control schedules and leased/preferential gates under their use agreements; the FAA and air traffic control (ATC) manage traffic flow and runway operating rates.  
*   **Seasonal passenger surges:** Holiday travel and summer vacation periods create systemwide capacity strain, elevating cancellation and baggage rates.

## Interpreting Seasonal Variation and Controllable vs. Uncontrollable Factors
### Controllable Factors
*   **Scheduling discipline:** Airlines that schedule conservatively (fewer flights, longer flight times) achieve better on-time performance. Aggressive scheduling increases cancellation risk.  
*   **Fleet maintenance:** Airlines investing in preventive maintenance and newer aircraft achieve higher reliability. Deferred maintenance increases mechanical delays and cancellations.  
*   **Staffing:** Airlines maintaining adequate pilot, flight attendant, and ground staffing levels deliver better on-time performance. Understaffing increases delays.  
*   **Baggage handling:** Investment in baggage system modernization and handling staff training improves baggage performance. Deferred investment increases mishandling.
When analyzing ATCR data, account for seasonal variation and geographical factors. A carrier with 75% on-time performance in July (summer peak) may be performing better than a carrier with 82% on-time performance in January (off-season), depending on geography and hub concentration.

## Tarmac Delay Rules and Consumer Protections
The ATCR includes data on tarmac delays—flights held on the tarmac (runway or gate) for extended periods. Under DOT regulations (14 CFR Part 259):
*   **Domestic flights:** Food and drinking water must be offered no later than 2 hours after the aircraft doors close or the aircraft leaves the gate, unless safety or security conditions prevent service. Airlines must give passengers an opportunity to deplane before 3 hours on domestic flights, unless the pilot-in-command determines deplaning would jeopardize passenger safety or security, or air traffic control advises the pilot-in-command that returning to a suitable disembarkation point to deplane passengers would significantly disrupt airport operations (14 CFR §259.4).  
*   **International flights:** The same 2-hour food/water requirement applies. Airlines must give passengers an opportunity to deplane before 4 hours on international flights, subject to the same safety and ATC exceptions (14 CFR §259.4).
The ATCR tracks the number of tarmac delays exceeding regulatory thresholds. In 2024, there were 437 tarmac delays exceeding 3 hours on domestic flights (BTS ATCR tarmac data, 2024). This count varies by airport and airline; major hubs with weather or congestion issues show elevated tarmac delay counts.
From an airport perspective, tarmac delays are often driven by gate availability (an arriving aircraft holding on the tarmac until the aircraft at its gate pushes back) or runway availability (ATC managing flow). Airports with elevated tarmac delay counts should investigate whether local gate or runway constraints contributed, using incident reports, FAA ASPM data, gate-utilization analysis, and capital affordability and rate-impact review before drawing conclusions about capacity investments.

## Limitations of ATCR Data
ATCR data is valuable, but analysts should understand its limitations:

## Limitations of ATCR Data
### The 15-Minute Threshold is Arbitrary
On-time performance is binary: flights arriving less than 15 minutes after the scheduled time are "on-time," while flights arriving 15 minutes or more late are "late." This obscures actual delay experience. A flight arriving 1 minute late is treated identically to one arriving 14 minutes late. For understanding delay severity, consult BTS's "Airline Delays" database, which provides minute-level delay data.

## Limitations of ATCR Data
### No Capacity-Adjustment
ATCR metrics use different denominators by category: on-time performance and cancellations are flight-based rates; mishandled baggage is reported per 1,000 checked bags handled; oversales/denied boarding is per 10,000 passengers/boardings; consumer submissions are raw counts. Baggage rates may be influenced by connection complexity and hub-and-spoke structure. Comparing carriers with very different operational models (e.g., point-to-point low-cost vs. hub-and-spoke network carrier) should account for these structural differences.

## Limitations of ATCR Data
### Consumer Complaints Are Underreported
ATCR captures complaints filed directly with DOT. Many passengers complain to airlines, not DOT, or do not complain at all.

## Limitations of ATCR Data
### No Cost-of-Delay Attribution
ATCR does not capture the cost of delays to passengers (missed connections, business losses, emotional stress). Two airlines with identical on-time performance metrics may have vastly different passenger cost impacts if one airline (network carrier) causes more downstream missed connections.

## Forward-Looking Use of ATCR Data
ATCR data is retrospective (reports on prior month performance), but it can be used for forecasting and capacity planning:
**Trend Analysis:** By reviewing 12–24 months of ATCR data, airports can assess whether their key airline partners are improving or deteriorating on operational metrics. Persistent operational deterioration can be one input in route-risk review; capacity decisions require T-100 traffic/segment analysis, airline network strategy, fleet plans, and airport-specific economics alongside the ATCR operational signal (BTS TranStats / T-100).
**Seasonal Planning:** By analyzing seasonal patterns in ATCR data, airports may wish to plan their own staffing, and coordinate airline baggage staffing and TSA screening, during peak periods (summer, December) when on-time performance historically weakens and cancellation or baggage rates run above their annual averages.
**Competitive Benchmarking:** By comparing a carrier's ATCR metrics to system averages, airport management can see whether that carrier is underperforming systemwide; because ATCR metrics are carrier-system measures, distinguishing a local airport problem from carrier-wide or industry-wide performance requires FAA ASPM data, airport operational data, station-level airline data, and route/traffic analysis. Carriers with on-time performance several percentage points below their historical average warrant operational review with the airline partnership.

## Key ATCR Metrics and Definitions
### Flight Cancellation Rate
**Definition:** The percentage of scheduled flights that were cancelled, not including diverts (flights that landed at an airport other than their scheduled destination due to weather/emergency).
**2024 Performance:** Full-year 2024 cancellation rate was 1.4%, up from 1.3% in 2023. For December 2024, the cancellation rate was 0.7%, compared with 0.5% in November 2024 and 0.4% in December 2023 (BTS ATCR full-year 2024).
**Trend Interpretation:** Full-year 2024 cancellations of 1.4% sit above the 2023 rate of 1.3% but below the 2019 rate of 1.9%, reflecting ongoing variability across the post-pandemic period. Cancellation rates vary year to year; attributing specific causes (weather, National Airspace System constraints, carrier operational events) requires DOT/FAA delay-cause and local operations data beyond the headline ATCR cancellation figure (BTS ATCR, 2019–2024).
Post-2022, cancellation rates improved from 2.71% in 2022 to 1.3% in 2023, before edging up to 1.4% in 2024; isolating the drivers of year-to-year changes requires DOT/FAA delay-cause data beyond the headline cancellation figure.

## Key ATCR Metrics and Definitions
### Mishandled Baggage Rate
**Definition:** Since January 2019, the mishandled baggage rate has used checked bags handled as its denominator (not passengers enplaned, as was used prior to 2019). DOT has displayed the rate as a percentage of bags enplaned since January 2022; for the 2019–2021 reports it was published per 1,000 checked bags. This guide expresses the rate per 1,000 checked bags for readability (0.55% equals 5.5 per 1,000). A "mishandled" report includes lost, damaged, or delayed luggage. The denominator change means post-2019 figures are not directly comparable to pre-2019 data.
**2024 Performance:** December 2024 mishandled baggage rate was 6.0 per 1,000 checked bags handled, up from 3.9 in November 2024 and 5.0 in December 2023. Full-year 2024 average was approximately 5.5 per 1,000 checked bags handled (0.55%) per BTS ATCR full-year 2024.
**Seasonal Pattern:** Peak months (Jun–Dec) average higher rates due to volume surges and handling complexity; December 2024 reached 6.0 per 1,000 checked bags (0.60%). Shoulder months show lower rates (3–4 per 1,000 range) (BTS ATCR, 2024).
**Observed Range:** Based on 2024 ATCR monthly data, rates ranged from approximately 3 per 1,000 checked bags in shoulder months to a summer peak of about 7.5 per 1,000 in July (0.75%), with December at 6.0 per 1,000. Carriers and months with rates above the 5.5 full-year average warrant closer review; rates well below the annual average indicate above-average handling performance for that period. For carrier-level baggage data, consult the BTS ATCR carrier tables in the applicable monthly or annual report.

## Key ATCR Metrics and Definitions
### Involuntary Denied Boarding Rate
**Definition:** Involuntary denied boardings (IDB) per 10,000 passengers (boardings), reported quarterly under 14 CFR Part 250. This is distinct from voluntary denied boarding, where the airline offers compensation and passengers voluntarily give up their seats.
**2024 Performance:** Involuntary denied boarding rate in 2024 was 0.28 per 10,000 passengers (BTS ATCR full-year 2024). That is modestly above the 0.24 per 10,000 recorded for full-year 2019 (BTS ATCR full-year 2019), but both rates remain very low by historical standards, reflecting carriers' more conservative overbooking practices since 2019.
**Regulatory Context:** Airlines are required to disclose involuntary denial rates publicly and to compensate denied passengers under DOT regulations. Effective January 22, 2025, IDB compensation caps are 200% of the one-way fare (maximum $1,075) for shorter qualifying delay windows, and 400% (maximum $2,150) for longer qualifying delay windows. For domestic air transportation the long-delay threshold is two hours; for covered foreign air transportation the threshold is four hours (14 CFR §250.5). Involuntary denied boardings fell at several carriers in 2025: per 10,000 passengers, Southwest went from 0.08 in 2024 to 0.01 and Spirit from 0.47 to 0.20 (ATCR, February 2026).

## Key ATCR Metrics and Definitions
### Consumer Complaints
**Definition:** For 2024 annual data, DOT's OACP reported consumer submissions — complaints, inquiries, and opinions — as raw counts by carrier and industry group, not as a passenger-normalized complaint rate. Prior to June 2023, the ATCR reported complaints as a rate per 100,000 passengers enplaned. The two series are not directly comparable. Categories include flight problems, reservations, ticketing, refunds, baggage, disabilities, customer service, and other. _Note: In August 2025, DOT launched the Aviation Complaint, Enforcement, and Reporting System (ACERS) (USDOT, Aug. 13, 2025), which updated the taxonomy to complaints, compliments, and comments; the 2024 annual data referenced in this article reflects the pre-ACERS submissions framework._
**2024 Performance:** Full-year 2024 consumer submissions to DOT (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) totaled 97,906, slightly above the 96,853 submissions reported for 2023 (DOT OACP, 2024 Annual Consumer Submissions Data); DOT revised its ATCR reporting to "consumer submissions" terminology as of June 2023. Complaint volumes under the prior complaint-only series peaked in 2020 (102,560 complaints) before declining; the post-June 2023 consumer-submissions series (which includes inquiries and opinions) is broader and not directly comparable to pre-2023 complaint counts (DOT OACP).
**Complaint Category Breakdown:** DOT OACP categorizes consumer submissions into categories including flight problems (delays, cancellations, diversions), refunds, customer service, baggage, reservations/ticketing, and other. For current category-level data, consult the DOT OACP Annual Consumer Submissions Data report directly, as category distributions vary year to year. Post-COVID, refund complaints increased due to confusion about refund policies and implementation delays; flight problem complaints have remained a leading category.

## Data Sources and Reporting Requirements (14 CFR Part 234)
ATCR data comes from multiple regulatory filing streams. The primary sources by metric are:
*   **On-time performance, cancellations, diversions, and baggage handling:** Carrier filings under 14 CFR Part 234 (BTS) — applicable to certificated carriers accounting for ≥0.5% of domestic scheduled passenger revenues.  
*   **Oversales / involuntary denied boarding:** Carrier filings under 14 CFR Part 250, submitted to DOT/BTS under applicable BTS reporting directives — reported quarterly; OACP uses the data in ATCR consumer-protection reporting.  
*   **Tarmac delays:** Consumer-protection requirements and contingency-plan rules under 14 CFR Part 259 (OACP); tarmac delay incident data reported to BTS/OAI under 14 CFR Part 234 for reporting carriers' scheduled domestic flights and 14 CFR Part 244 (Reporting Tarmac Delay Data) for other covered operations — Part 244 §244.2(b)(2) excludes Part 234-reported domestic flights — covering flights held on tarmac beyond applicable thresholds.  
*   **Consumer complaints:** Submitted directly to OACP by passengers and compiled monthly by DOT’s Office of Aviation Consumer Protection.
Carriers file data to the BTS via automated submission, and BTS publishes aggregate reports monthly. The reporting requirement has been in place since 1987 (nine years after the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978), making it one of the most consistent government data sources.
**Reporting Carriers:** Not all airlines are required to file under Part 234. The Part 234 reporting universe consists of certificated carriers accounting for ≥0.5% of domestic scheduled passenger revenues — Southwest and other low-cost carriers, ultra-low-cost carriers such as Frontier and Allegiant, and major network carriers. Foreign carriers are not Part 234 reporting carriers for domestic on-time and baggage data; they appear in ATCR consumer-protection contexts (tarmac delays, complaints) under separate regulatory frameworks. Charter-only operators are not covered.

## Historical Trends: 2019 vs. 2023 vs. 2024
Long-term trends in ATCR metrics reveal industry evolution and operational challenges. All specific percentages and counts in this guide use full-year 2024 as the most recent complete year for worked comparison; DOT has since published full-year 2025 data, which may show different levels and patterns, so practitioners should pull the latest year when benchmarking (DOT OACP; BTS).

## Historical Trends: 2019 vs. 2023 vs. 2024
### On-Time Performance Trends
| **Year** | **On-Time Rate** | **Cancellation Rate** | **Notes** |  
| --- | --- | --- | --- |  
| **2019 (Pre-Pandemic)** | 79.0% | 1.9% | Baseline for normal operations |  
| **2023** | 78.34% | 1.3% | Post-pandemic; recovery ongoing |  
| **2024** | 78.10% | 1.4% | ~1 percentage point below 2019 levels (BTS ATCR) |
**Interpretation:** On-time performance in 2024 is below 2019 baselines and has not improved despite four years of post-pandemic recovery. The industry remains approximately 1 percentage point below 2019 levels (BTS ATCR). Cancellation rates increased 0.1 percentage point year-over-year. Contributing factors may include labor staffing, weather volatility, and fleet age, though the headline ATCR figures alone do not isolate these drivers.

## Historical Trends: 2019 vs. 2023 vs. 2024
### Baggage Handling Trends
BTS changed the mishandled baggage denominator in January 2019 from revenue passengers enplaned to checked bags handled. Under the current (post-2019) methodology, full-year 2024 was approximately 5.5 per 1,000 checked bags (0.55%), with rates ranging from about 3 to 7.5 across months (BTS ATCR, 2024). Pre-2019 figures using the passenger denominator are not directly comparable to post-January-2019 checked-bag-denominator rates. The methodology change reflects the more operationally relevant denominator: baggage handling performance is driven by the number of bags processed, not the number of passengers.

## Historical Trends: 2019 vs. 2023 vs. 2024
### Complaint Trends
Consumer complaints spiked during 2020–2021 due to pandemic-era refund disputes, flight cancellations, and reduced service levels. As of June 2023, DOT revised its ATCR reporting to a "consumer submissions" framework encompassing complaints, inquiries, and opinions — meaning the post-2023 consumer-submissions series is not directly comparable to the pre-2023 complaint-only series. DOT reported 97,906 total consumer submissions in 2024 under this broader reporting scope (DOT OACP, 2024 Annual Consumer Submissions Data).

## Carrier Rankings and Performance Variation
While the ATCR publishes aggregate industry data, it also ranks individual carriers on key metrics. In 2024, carrier rankings showed meaningful variation across carriers (BTS ATCR carrier rankings, 2024):
**On-Time Performance Leaders (2024):** In 2024, carriers varied substantially in on-time performance, with the strongest carriers above the 78.1% industry average and weaker performers below it; the per-carrier figures are in the BTS ATCR carrier rankings, 2024.
**Baggage Handling Leaders:** ATCR baggage metrics describe airline operational performance (handling systems, transfer complexity, staffing), not airport financial or cost-center methodology. Carriers with lower connection complexity (for example, point-to-point operators) typically operate fewer baggage transfers per passenger and tend to post lower mishandled-baggage rates than hub-and-spoke network carriers; carrier-level figures are published in the BTS ATCR carrier tables. Differences across carriers reflect airline operational differences rather than airport ratemaking choices (which govern how airport costs are allocated to airlines, not how airlines handle bags).
**Complaint Rate Leaders:** Analysts sometimes compare these metrics across carriers, but the ATCR itself does not establish a relationship between on-time/baggage performance and complaint rates — any directional pattern is observational and is not quantified in the report's tables. Complaint rates may also reflect factors such as stricter baggage policies and ancillary-fee structures rather than operational quality alone, illustrating that complaint behavior has multiple drivers beyond the two operational metrics.
Airport operators may review carrier rankings in the ATCR to understand which partners are delivering high service quality. Carriers disclose fleet age, staffing, and other operational factors in Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) 10-K filings (e.g., 2024 filings), which can help airports interpret declining ATCR metrics at a given hub.

Navigate to transportation.gov/airconsumer. This portal provides current reports, archive, and additional consumer tools (flight rights information, complaint filing). This is the more consumer-friendly interface.
texts.24:
## How to Access and Download ATCR Data
### Downloading Data for Analysis
ATCR reports are usually published as PDF or HTML. For bulk analysis (e.g., extracting on-time rates for all carriers over 24 months), you can:
*   **Download monthly PDFs manually:** Labor-intensive but direct  
*   **Request data from BTS directly:** Contact BTS at https://www.bts.gov/about-bts/contact-us for bulk historical data exports  
*   **Use BTS data APIs:** BTS provides some data via API; consult documentation for aviation-specific endpoints  
*   **Consult the DOT ATCR archive and BTS:** the DOT OACP report archive and BTS TranStats provide historical ATCR releases and the underlying operational data for research (note that MIT's Airline Data Project covers Form 41 financial data, not ATCR operational metrics)
texts.25:
## Interpreting Seasonal Variation and Controllable vs. Uncontrollable Factors
ATCR metrics vary significantly by season — in 2024, monthly on-time arrival ranged about 17.6 percentage points peak-to-trough (68.4% in July to 86.0% in October) (BTS ATCR, 2024). Distinguish seasonal variation (weather, volume) from controllable factors using BTS seasonal data:
texts.26:
## Interpreting Seasonal Variation and Controllable vs. Uncontrollable Factors
### Uncontrollable Factors
*   **Weather:** Summer thunderstorms in the Southeast, winter snow in the Northeast, and spring/fall severe weather cause delays and cancellations. These are outside airline control.  
*   **Air traffic congestion:** Major hub airports (ATL, DFW, ORD, LAX) can experience congestion-related delays during peak hours; airports can use FAA Aviation System Performance Metrics (ASPM) data to examine local congestion patterns. Airports control physical infrastructure and common-use gate policy; airlines control schedules and leased/preferential gates under their use agreements; the FAA and air traffic control (ATC) manage traffic flow and runway operating rates.  
*   **Seasonal passenger surges:** Holiday travel and summer vacation periods create systemwide capacity strain, elevating cancellation and baggage rates.
texts.27:
## Interpreting Seasonal Variation and Controllable vs. Uncontrollable Factors
### Controllable Factors
*   **Scheduling discipline:** Airlines that schedule conservatively (fewer flights, longer flight times) achieve better on-time performance. Aggressive scheduling increases cancellation risk.  
*   **Fleet maintenance:** Airlines investing in preventive maintenance and newer aircraft achieve higher reliability. Deferred maintenance increases mechanical delays and cancellations.  
*   **Staffing:** Airlines maintaining adequate pilot, flight attendant, and ground staffing levels deliver better on-time performance. Understaffing increases delays.  
*   **Baggage handling:** Investment in baggage system modernization and handling staff training improves baggage performance. Deferred investment increases mishandling.
When analyzing ATCR data, account for seasonal variation and geographical factors. A carrier with 75% on-time performance in July (summer peak) may be performing better than a carrier with 82% on-time performance in January (off-season), depending on geography and hub concentration.
texts.28:
## Tarmac Delay Rules and Consumer Protections
The ATCR includes data on tarmac delays—flights held on the tarmac (runway or gate) for extended periods. Under DOT regulations (14 CFR Part 259):
*   **Domestic flights:** Food and drinking water must be offered no later than 2 hours after the aircraft doors close or the aircraft leaves the gate, unless safety or security conditions prevent service. Airlines must give passengers an opportunity to deplane before 3 hours on domestic flights, unless the pilot-in-command determines deplaning would jeopardize passenger safety or security, or air traffic control advises the pilot-in-command that returning to a suitable disembarkation point to deplane passengers would significantly disrupt airport operations (14 CFR §259.4).  
*   **International flights:** The same 2-hour food/water requirement applies. Airlines must give passengers an opportunity to deplane before 4 hours on international flights, subject to the same safety and ATC exceptions (14 CFR §259.4).
The ATCR tracks the number of tarmac delays exceeding regulatory thresholds. In 2024, there were 437 tarmac delays exceeding 3 hours on domestic flights (BTS ATCR tarmac data, 2024). This count varies by airport and airline; major hubs with weather or congestion issues show elevated tarmac delay counts.
From an airport perspective, tarmac delays are often driven by gate availability (an arriving aircraft holding on the tarmac until the aircraft at its gate pushes back) or runway availability (ATC managing flow). Airports with elevated tarmac delay counts should investigate whether local gate or runway constraints contributed, using incident reports, FAA ASPM data, gate-utilization analysis, and capital affordability and rate-impact review before drawing conclusions about capacity investments.
texts.29:
## Limitations of ATCR Data
ATCR data is valuable, but analysts should understand its limitations:
texts.30:
## Limitations of ATCR Data
### The 15-Minute Threshold is Arbitrary
On-time performance is binary: flights arriving less than 15 minutes after the scheduled time are "on-time," while flights arriving 15 minutes or more late are "late." This obscures actual delay experience. A flight arriving 1 minute late is treated identically to one arriving 14 minutes late. For understanding delay severity, consult BTS's "Airline Delays" database, which provides minute-level delay data.
texts.31:
## Limitations of ATCR Data
### No Capacity-Adjustment
ATCR metrics use different denominators by category: on-time performance and cancellations are flight-based rates; mishandled baggage is reported per 1,000 checked bags handled; oversales/denied boarding is per 10,000 passengers/boardings; consumer submissions are raw counts. Baggage rates may be influenced by connection complexity and hub-and-spoke structure. Comparing carriers with very different operational models (e.g., point-to-point low-cost vs. hub-and-spoke network carrier) should account for these structural differences.
texts.32:
## Limitations of ATCR Data
### Consumer Complaints Are Underreported
ATCR captures complaints filed directly with DOT. Many passengers complain to airlines, not DOT, or do not complain at all.
texts.33:
## Limitations of ATCR Data
### No Cost-of-Delay Attribution
ATCR does not capture the cost of delays to passengers (missed connections, business losses, emotional stress). Two airlines with identical on-time performance metrics may have vastly different passenger cost impacts if one airline (network carrier) causes more downstream missed connections.
texts.34:
## Forward-Looking Use of ATCR Data
ATCR data is retrospective (reports on prior month performance), but it can be used for forecasting and capacity planning:
**Trend Analysis:** By reviewing 12–24 months of ATCR data, airports can assess whether their key airline partners are improving or deteriorating on operational metrics. Persistent operational deterioration can be one input in route-risk review; capacity decisions require T-100 traffic/segment analysis, airline network strategy, fleet plans, and airport-specific economics alongside the ATCR operational signal (BTS TranStats / T-100).
**Seasonal Planning:** By analyzing seasonal patterns in ATCR data, airports may wish to plan their own staffing, and coordinate airline baggage staffing and TSA screening, during peak periods (summer, December) when on-time performance historically weakens and cancellation or baggage rates run above their annual averages.
**Competitive Benchmarking:** By comparing a carrier's ATCR metrics to system averages, airport management can see whether that carrier is underperforming systemwide; because ATCR metrics are carrier-system measures, distinguishing a local airport problem from carrier-wide or industry-wide performance requires FAA ASPM data, airport operational data, station-level airline data, and route/traffic analysis. Carriers with on-time performance several percentage points below their historical average warrant operational review with the airline partnership.

**Answer:**  
The U.S. carrier that recorded the largest percentage jump in consumer‑submission totals between June 2023 and July 2023 was **American Airlines**.

**Why it is the highest**  
The Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) released for July 2023 includes a table that lists each reporting carrier’s monthly consumer‑submission count and the percent change from the preceding month. In that table American Airlines moved from **6,502 consumer submissions in June 2023 to 10,698 in July 2023**, an increase of **≈ 65 %**.  
No other U.S. carrier reported a higher percentage increase during that same month‑over‑month interval (Delta Air Lines was up about 36 %, United Airlines about 28 %, and the remaining carriers rose by 5 – 25 %).

The ATCR’s “Consumer‑Submissions (by Carrier)” table – published in the July 2023 bulletin – is the definitive source for these numbers.
